analogy.p: Think of a compound measure as how fast a tap fills a bath: so many litres per minute. If you know the rate and the time, you can find how much water is in the bath (amount = rate × time), and if you know the amount and the rate you can find the time. Density is like how many marbles you can cram into every cubic centimetre, and pressure is like how sharply a force is concentrated onto a patch of floor. The analogy breaks down because a real tap rate can vary, whereas the formulae assume the rate is constant or give only an average.
analogy.t: Rates are like a tap and a bath

bullets: A compound measure is a measure made by dividing (or sometimes multiplying) two different measures, e.g. distance ÷ time = speed.
The unit of the compound measure is built from the two units used: km ÷ h = **km/h**, g ÷ cm³ = **g/cm³**, N ÷ m² = **N/m²**.

Other everyday compound measures: **rate of pay** (£ per hour), **unit price** (pence per 100 g), **fuel consumption** (litres per 100 km), **flow rate** (litres per minute) and **population density** (people per km²).
Rates describe how fast one quantity changes with another, which links directly to **rates of change** and the gradient of a graph.
You are expected to use the formulae, rearrange them, and convert between compound units (see Units and conversions).
Higher tier: expect multi-step problems that combine several rates, or that ask you to explain why a calculation using an average of two speeds is wrong.
core.h: What a compound measure is and what the specification requires
core.p: The Edexcel specification (Ratio, proportion and rates of change) requires you to **use compound units such as speed, rates of pay, unit pricing, density and pressure**. A compound measure combines two different quantities into a single **rate**: it tells you how much of one quantity there is **for each one** of another. Whenever you see the word 'per' (kilometres per hour, pounds per kilogram, grams per cubic centimetre) you are looking at a compound unit. Mark schemes reward correct formulae, consistent units and a unit on the answer.

bullets: **S = D ÷ T**, **D = S × T**, **T = D ÷ S**. A formula triangle with D at the top and S and T at the bottom helps you rearrange: cover what you want.
Units: km/h or mph for road journeys, m/s for science and short times.
Example: 150 km in 2.5 hours gives 150 ÷ 2.5 = 60 km/h.
Example: time for 90 km at 45 km/h = 90 ÷ 45 = 2 hours.
Example: 20 minutes at 36 km/h gives 36 × (20 ÷ 60) = 12 km.
**Average speed** over a whole journey = **total distance ÷ total time**. It includes any stops if the total time includes them.
A speed given as a decimal of hours needs care: 1.25 h = 1 hour 15 minutes, not 1 h 25 min.
Always sense check: a walker travels at about 5 km/h, a cyclist about 20 km/h, a car about 50 to 110 km/h.
core.p: **Speed** is how far something travels in each unit of time. For constant speed the three quantities are linked by **speed = distance ÷ time**, and rearranging gives **distance = speed × time** and **time = distance ÷ speed**. Using these correctly depends on the units matching: if speed is in km/h then distance must be in km and time in hours. When the time is given in minutes you must convert it (divide by 60) before using it.

bullets: Method: find the time for each part (time = distance ÷ speed), add the distances and the times, then divide total distance by total time.
Example: out at 60 km/h and back at 40 km/h over the same 120 km: times are 2 h and 3 h, total distance 240 km, total time 5 h, average = 240 ÷ 5 = **48 km/h**.
Why not 50 km/h? You spend longer at the lower speed, so the average is pulled towards 40.
If equal **times** are spent at each speed, then the mean of the speeds is correct (e.g. 1 hour at 60 and 1 hour at 40 gives 50 km/h), but for equal **distances** it is not.
If the question does not give a distance, pick a convenient one (such as the lowest common multiple of the two speeds) and say so.
Include waiting time if the question asks for the average speed for the whole journey including a stop.
A speed in m/s can be converted to km/h by × 3.6 and the reverse by ÷ 3.6.
core.h: Average speed and the common trap
core.p: The most frequent error in this topic is finding an average speed by averaging the speeds. The correct method is always **total distance ÷ total time**. If a journey is split into sections at different speeds, you need the time for every section first. If a driver goes somewhere at 60 km/h and returns at 40 km/h, the average speed is **not** 50 km/h, because more time is spent travelling at the slower speed.

bullets: A **straight line sloping upwards** means constant speed; the steeper the line, the faster the speed.
A **horizontal (flat) line** means the object is stationary (distance is not changing).
A **line sloping downwards** means the object is returning towards the start.
Gradient = vertical change ÷ horizontal change = (change in distance) ÷ (change in time) = speed. Use a large triangle on the line for accuracy.
Units: if the axes are km and hours, the gradient is in km/h. Check the axis scales before calculating.
**Average speed** for the whole journey = total distance travelled ÷ total time (not displacement). A return journey ends at 0 on the graph but the distance travelled is the sum of both parts.
Higher tier: for a **curve**, the speed at an instant is estimated by drawing a **tangent** and finding its gradient; a curve getting steeper means accelerating.
Common marking points: 'the object stops for 1 hour', 'travels at 30 km/h for the first hour', 'returns at a slower speed'.
core.p: A **distance-time graph** shows how far an object is from its start as time passes. Time goes on the **horizontal axis** and distance on the **vertical axis**. The **gradient** of the line is the **speed**, so you can read speeds straight from a graph by working out 'change in distance ÷ change in time'. This is one of the clearest examples of a rate of change, and it is a regular exam question.

bullets: **ρ = m ÷ V**, **m = ρ × V**, **V = m ÷ ρ**. Make sure mass and volume units match the density unit (g with cm³, kg with m³).
Example: 450 g of a metal occupies 50 cm³, so density = 450 ÷ 50 = 9 g/cm³.
Example: concrete of density 2400 kg/m³ and volume 2.5 m³ has mass 2400 × 2.5 = 6000 kg.
Example: 360 g of a liquid of density 0.9 g/cm³ has volume 360 ÷ 0.9 = 400 cm³.
Water has a density of about **1 g/cm³** (1000 kg/m³); objects less dense than water float.
**1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³**, so convert before comparing if the units differ.
For a composite material, find the **total mass** and the **total volume** and divide: you cannot average the two densities unless the volumes are equal.
Volume may need calculating first from dimensions (e.g. prism or cylinder), then convert cm³ and m³ carefully.
core.p: **Density** is the **mass per unit volume** of a substance, and it tells you how tightly packed the matter is. The formula is **density = mass ÷ volume**, written ρ = m/V, with units such as g/cm³ or kg/m³. Two objects of the same size can have very different masses if they are made of different materials, and density is the property that explains this. Density is a compound measure because it combines mass and volume.

bullets: **P = F ÷ A**, **F = P × A**, **A = F ÷ P**. Force is in newtons (N), area in m² (or cm²) and pressure in N/m² (or N/cm²).
Example: a force of 600 N on 0.3 m² gives 600 ÷ 0.3 = 2000 N/m².
Example: 5000 N/m² acting on 0.4 m² gives a force of 5000 × 0.4 = 2000 N.
Example: pressure 800 N/m², force 200 N gives area 200 ÷ 800 = 0.25 m².
To **increase** pressure, increase the force or decrease the area; to **decrease** pressure, spread the force over a larger area.
**1 N/cm² = 10 000 N/m²** because 1 m² = 10 000 cm².
Weight is a force measured in newtons, so do not confuse it with mass in kg; maths questions normally give the force directly.
If the object has several faces, the **area in contact** with the ground is the one to use.
core.p: **Pressure** is the **force acting per unit area**, so **pressure = force ÷ area**. It is measured in **newtons per square metre (N/m²)**, also called **pascals (Pa)**. The same force produces a larger pressure on a smaller area, which is why a knife cuts better when it is sharp and why snow shoes stop you sinking. Pressure is a compound measure of force and area, and Edexcel questions use it with simple numbers.

bullets: **Rate of pay**: pay = hourly rate × hours. Example: 35 hours at £12 plus 5 hours at time-and-a-half (£18) = 420 + 90 = £510.
**Overtime** at 'time and a half' means 1.5 × normal rate; 'double time' means 2 × the normal rate.
**Unit price** (best buy): divide the price by the quantity to compare. 750 ml for £1.80 = 24p per 100 ml; 1.2 litres for £2.76 = 23p per 100 ml, so the larger bottle is the better buy.
Compare using the **same unit** (per 100 ml, per kg), and say which is the better value.
**Fuel consumption**: litres per 100 km or miles per gallon; **flow rate**: litres per minute, so time = volume ÷ rate.
**Population density** = number of people ÷ area, e.g. 54 000 people on 30 km² is 1800 people per km².
**Exchange rate** is a rate of currency per pound; **interest rate** is a percentage per year.
Link to other topics: direct proportion, because a constant rate means the graph is a straight line through the origin.
core.h: Rates of pay, unit pricing and other rates
core.p: Many practical problems are rates in disguise. A **rate of pay** is money per hour, a **unit price** is the cost for one unit of weight or volume, and a **best buy** compares unit prices. These are all compound measures. The method is to find the amount **per one unit** (the unit rate) and then scale it up or down. Remember to give money in pounds and pence to 2 decimal places.

bullets: For a formula such as S = D ÷ T, the triangle has D on top and S and T underneath; **cover** the one you want and read what is left.
If the unit of the answer is 'per', the calculation is a **division**. If you want the total quantity, multiply the rate by the quantity.
Unit analysis: m/s × s = m, so distance = speed × time gives metres. If your units do not combine to give the expected unit, you have used the wrong formula.
Rearranging with algebra: from ρ = m/V multiply both sides by V to give m = ρV; then divide by ρ to give V = m/ρ.
Do not mix units: if the speed is in m/s and the time is in minutes, change the minutes to seconds first.
**Acceleration** is another compound measure: change in speed ÷ time, in m/s² (metres per second per second).
The method 'find the rate for one, then scale' works for every rate problem.
Check that the answer has the **right size** and the **right unit** before moving on.
core.h: Formula triangles, rearranging and unit analysis
core.p: You can recall all three versions of a compound-measure formula with a **formula triangle**, but you must also understand why the formula works. The unit of the compound measure tells you the formula: km/h means km **divided by** h, g/cm³ means g **divided by** cm³. Reading the unit as a sentence ('so many kilometres **per** hour') lets you rebuild the formula if you forget it in the exam, which is a Higher tier skill.

bullets: Break the problem into stages and **record the time for each stage** before you add.
Convert minutes to hours when working in km/h: 45 minutes = 0.75 hours; 2 h 20 min = 2⅓ hours (use the fraction 7/3 for exact work).
Example: 15 km at 20 km/h then 10 km at 5 km/h. Times: 0.75 h and 2 h. Total 25 km in 2.75 h gives average = 25 ÷ 2.75 = 9.09 km/h (to 3 s.f.).
**Relative stories**: two people walking towards each other close the gap at the **sum** of their speeds.
Time of arrival: add the journey time to the start time using hours and minutes, not decimals.
**Cost problems**: cost = rate × quantity, e.g. 4.5 litres per minute for 20 minutes is 90 litres.
State assumptions such as 'constant speed' when a question needs them.
Link to other topics: algebra (forming and solving equations from rates), ratio and proportion.
core.p: Higher tier questions rarely test one formula in isolation. They chain several: first convert a unit, then calculate a time, then find an average speed or a cost. The safe approach is to write down each quantity you need with its unit, decide which formula links the known and unknown, and calculate step by step. Marks are given for each correct step even if the final answer is wrong.

bullets: **km/h to m/s**: ÷ 3.6. Example: 90 km/h = 25 m/s.
**m/s to km/h**: × 3.6. Example: 8 m/s = 28.8 km/h.
**g/cm³ to kg/m³**: × 1000. Example: 2.7 g/cm³ = 2700 kg/m³.
**N/cm² to N/m²**: × 10 000. Example: 0.5 N/cm² = 5000 N/m² (5000 Pa).
**Litres per minute to cm³ per second**: × 1000 ÷ 60. Example: 6 litres/min = 100 cm³/s.
**£ per kg to pence per g**: £1 per kg is 100p per 1000 g = 0.1p per g.
Write the working in steps, e.g. 90 km/h = 90 000 m per hour = 90 000 ÷ 3600 m/s = 25 m/s.
Before you finish, check that the number has moved in the expected direction.
core.p: Compound units are converted by converting each part of the unit separately. You change the top unit, then the bottom unit, and combine the factors. Writing the conversion as a chain of fractions with the units shown lets you cancel the units and avoid mistakes. This is why mixed-unit problems (such as km/h to m/s) are worth practising until they are automatic.

bullets: **Direct proportion** y = kx: the compound measure is k (for distance and time, k = speed).
On a graph of mass (vertical) against volume (horizontal), the **gradient is the density** in g/cm³.
On a graph of cost against quantity, the gradient is the unit price.
If the graph does not pass through the origin, there is a fixed charge (e.g. a taxi starting fee), and the gradient is still the rate per unit.
On a curved graph, the **rate of change at a point** equals the gradient of the **tangent** at that point.
A rate staying constant means a straight line; a changing rate gives a curve.
Link to other topics: gradient and equations of straight lines, velocity-time graphs (gradient = acceleration, area = distance), and growth and decay.
Always give the units of a gradient as 'unit of y per unit of x'.
core.p: A compound measure is a **constant of proportionality**. When distance is directly proportional to time, the constant is the speed; when mass is directly proportional to volume, the constant is the density. Plotting the two quantities gives a **straight line through the origin** whose **gradient is the rate**. For Higher tier you must interpret gradients as rates of change, including on non-linear graphs, where the rate at a point is found with a tangent.

bullets: Write the **formula first**, then substitute with units, then the answer with units.
Convert awkward units **before** substituting (minutes to hours, cm to m, g to kg).
Keep full calculator values until the end and give the final answer to a sensible accuracy.
Check the answer using the rearranged formula (e.g. distance ÷ time gives back the speed).
Use estimation: 400 g of metal in 50 cm³ must be a bit less than 10 g/cm³ (it is 8 g/cm³).
If a question says 'give a reason', refer to the formula or the calculation (e.g. 'because the larger area gives a smaller pressure').
Remember best-buy answers need a conclusion: write which is better value and quote the unit prices.
Do not forget units on the final answer and write 'per' units correctly (km/h, not km per h twice).
core.p: Compound measure questions are usually 2 to 4 marks, and the marks are earned in a predictable way: one for the correct formula or division, one for the numerical working, and one for the answer with a unit. In a 'show that' or reasoning question the final mark is for a clear explanation, such as 'the average speed is total distance divided by total time, not the mean of the two speeds'. Developing a routine saves marks.

exam: Command words: **'Work out'** needs numerical working and a unit; **'Show that'** needs every step and a statement of the given result; **'Explain'** needs a reason referring to the formula.

Typical marks: 2 marks for a one-step formula with unit (e.g. density = mass ÷ volume), 3 marks for a two-stage problem (convert then calculate) and 4 marks for multi-step average-speed or composite density questions.
Write the formula first: this alone can earn a method mark.
For **average speed** always show total distance and total time; use 'total distance ÷ total time' in the explanation.
Convert times to hours (minutes ÷ 60) before using km/h; write fractions such as 1/3 h for exact working.
On **distance-time graphs** draw a large gradient triangle, read the values from the axes and include units (km/h or m/s).
Describing graph sections: say 'travelling at a constant speed of ...', 'stopped for ... hours', 'returning to the start at ...'.
For **best-buy** questions work out the cost per unit for each, compare, and write a conclusion.
For **density** of a mixture add the masses and volumes separately; state the unit.
For **pressure** explain with 'the force is spread over a larger area so the pressure is smaller'.
Use the sense check, e.g. a car cannot average 600 km/h; check you used hours and not minutes.

mistakes.r: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time. Find the time for each part first (for 60 and 40 km/h over equal distances the answer is 48 km/h).
mistakes.w: Finding average speed by adding two speeds and dividing by 2 (e.g. (60 + 40) ÷ 2 = 50).

mistakes.r: Convert time to hours first (÷ 60), e.g. 30 minutes = 0.5 h; or convert the speed to km per minute.
mistakes.w: Using minutes directly in a speed calculation with km/h.

mistakes.r: 2 h 30 min = 2.5 hours; divide the minutes by 60.
Find the total mass and the total volume, then divide: density = total mass ÷ total volume.
mistakes.w: Averaging two densities to find the density of a mixture.

mistakes.r: Use the unit as a check: g/cm³ means mass divided by volume.
mistakes.w: Getting the formula the wrong way round, e.g. density = volume ÷ mass.

mistakes.r: Convert so that mass and volume units match the density unit before substituting.
mistakes.w: Mixing units, such as mass in kg with density in g/cm³.

mistakes.r: Pressure = force ÷ area, so for the same force a larger area gives a smaller pressure.
mistakes.w: Saying pressure is larger when the area is larger.

mistakes.r: Gradient = change in distance ÷ change in time using the axis values and units.
mistakes.w: Reading the gradient of a distance-time graph without using the scales.

mistakes.r: Work out the unit price (e.g. per 100 g) for each and compare; state which is better value.
mistakes.w: Finding best buy by comparing prices only.

mistakes.r: Always write units on the answer: km/h, g/cm³, N/m² (Pa).
mistakes.w: Leaving out units or writing the wrong compound unit.

summary: Edexcel requires you to use compound units and measures such as speed, rates of pay, unit pricing, density and pressure, including rearranging the formulae and converting compound units. It matters because rates of change are a core Higher theme and these questions hide marks in unit conversions, average speed and best-buy reasoning.

terms.d: A measure formed by combining two different quantities, such as distance and time, to give a rate.
A comparison of two different quantities expressed as an amount per one unit of the other, e.g. 60 km per 1 hour.
The distance travelled per unit of time: speed = distance ÷ time.
Total distance travelled divided by total time taken.
Speed that does not change, shown by a straight line on a distance-time graph.
A graph with time on the horizontal axis and distance on the vertical axis; gradient = speed.
The steepness of a line: change in vertical ÷ change in horizontal; it represents the rate of change.
Mass per unit volume: density = mass ÷ volume, in g/cm³ or kg/m³.
Force per unit area: pressure = force ÷ area, in N/m² (pascals).
The unit of pressure; 1 Pa = 1 N/m².
The cost per single unit (e.g. per 100 g or per litre), used to find the best buy.
The amount earned per unit of time, e.g. £12 per hour.
The volume of fluid that passes per unit of time, e.g. litres per minute.
How quickly one quantity changes compared with another; shown by the gradient of a graph.
A straight line that touches a curve at one point; its gradient estimates the rate of change at that point.

worked.ans: 48 km/h (not 50 km/h, because more time is spent at the lower speed)
worked.q: Sam drives from home to a town at an average speed of 60 km/h and returns by the same route at 40 km/h. Work out his average speed for the whole journey. (3 marks)
steps: Choose a distance for each leg, e.g. 120 km (any distance gives the same answer).
Out: time = 120 ÷ 60 = 2 h. Back: time = 120 ÷ 40 = 3 h. [M1]
Total distance = 240 km; total time = 5 h. [M1]

worked.ans: 10 g/cm³ (this equals the mean of 8 and 12 only because the two volumes happen to be equal)
worked.q: A metal block is made by joining 200 g of metal A (density 8 g/cm³) and 300 g of metal B (density 12 g/cm³). Work out the density of the mixture. (4 marks)
steps: Volume of A = mass ÷ density = 200 ÷ 8 = 25 cm³. [M1]
Total mass = 500 g; total volume = 25 + 25 = 50 cm³. [M1]

worked.ans: 2000 N/m² on the large face and 6000 N/m² on the small face; the smaller face gives the greater pressure.
worked.q: A block weighing 600 N rests on a flat surface. Its larger face has area 0.3 m² and its smaller face has area 0.1 m². (a) Work out the pressure when it rests on each face. (b) Explain which face gives the greater pressure. (4 marks)
steps: (b) The same force is spread over a smaller area, so the pressure is greater (three times as large). [B1]
